title: Wittgenstein
summary: Wittgenstein was an Austrian-British philosopher and one of the most influential thinkers of the 20th century. In his early work he tried to draw the limits of what can be said clearly; in his later work he showed that the meaning of words lies in how we use them in living “language-games.” He understood philosophy as therapy: not building theories but untangling the knots our language ties us in.
onEmotions: Wittgenstein wrote no theory of feelings, but he changed a great deal about how we think of them. He showed that words for feelings are not labels on objects locked in the “box” of the soul but part of a shared life: we learn to say “it hurts” in place of a cry, and that is why feelings can be shared. He distinguished what is said from what is shown: the most important things — ethics, the meaning of life, beauty — cannot be put into words but show themselves in how a person lives. His philosophy is therapy: he compared many torments of the mind to a fly in a fly-bottle, which needs not new knowledge but to be shown the way out.

anxiety.text: A fly beats against the wall of a glass fly-bottle though the neck is open — this was Wittgenstein's image for a mind tangled in its own questions. Anxiety often sounds just like that: an endless “what if…?” Wittgenstein believed that many tormenting questions — in philosophy and in life — arise not because the world is mysterious but because the forms of our language lead us astray. He called this the “bewitchment” of our intelligence by language. A question looks as if it has an answer, and the mind beats against the glass again and again. Wittgenstein saw the task of philosophy as therapy: not to solve such a question but to see how it is built — and then it loses its power. Then not every “what if…” demands an answer. Sometimes it's enough to notice that it's a trap, and that the way out was right there.
anxiety.practice: Write down your anxious question and ask yourself: does it have an answer that can be found out now? If not, label it: “fly-bottle question.”

quote.text: What is your aim in philosophy? — To shew the fly the way out of the fly-bottle.
quote.author: Ludwig Wittgenstein

fear.text: “I am afraid” — Wittgenstein noticed that these words are often not a report, like “it's raining outside,” but more like a cry, like flinching. There is nothing shameful in fear, natural and strong as it is. This observation may help right now. He wrote that we learn to say words for sensations in place of immediate exclamations and gestures. This is an important observation: when you say “I'm scared,” you are not just reporting a fact, you are also doing something with your fear — bringing it outward, into the shared world, where it can be heard. If so, naming fear is already a small step toward not being alone with it.
fear.practice: Say aloud — to yourself or to someone nearby: “I'm scared right now.” For Wittgenstein this is not a report but a cry brought out into the shared world. Notice what changes.

sadness.text: The facts are the same, yet the whole world is different — that is one way to retell a strange remark of Wittgenstein's. Sadness can color everything around you in just this way. In the Tractatus Wittgenstein made an unusual remark: a good or bad will changes not the facts of the world but its limits, so that the world as a whole, as it were, waxes or wanes. Sadness works in a similar way: objects and events stay the same, but the whole world looks different, as if the lighting had changed. In this light, sadness is not one more fact to be fixed but the color in which everything is seen right now. Such a view lifts the pressure to “find the cause and eliminate it.” You can acknowledge that the world is colored this way right now, and wait for the light to change.
sadness.practice: Look out of the window for a minute and notice how sadness colors what you see: the sky, faces, the street. The facts are the same — the lighting changes.

quote.text: The world of the happy man is a different one from that of the unhappy man.
quote.author: Ludwig Wittgenstein

grief.text: A pattern that recurs, with different variations, in the weave of life — this is how Wittgenstein described grief. It is enormous and often finds no words. It returns in familiar places, in words, in rituals. This helps explain why grief doesn't “pass” on schedule: it is woven into life. In the Tractatus Wittgenstein distinguished what can be said from what can only show itself. The silence he speaks of is not emptiness but respect for what is larger than words. If you can't manage to express your grief, it doesn't mean you are doing something wrong. Sometimes love shows itself precisely in silence.
grief.practice: Find an object or a place connected with the one you lost and stay beside it for a minute in silence. What cannot be said can show itself.

quote.text: What we cannot speak about we must pass over in silence.
quote.author: Ludwig Wittgenstein

loneliness.text: Imagine that everyone has a box with a “beetle” in it and no one can look into anyone else's — with this thought experiment in the Philosophical Investigations Wittgenstein begins his argument with the picture of loneliness. Loneliness sometimes feels exactly like that: as though your experiences are locked inside and no one can understand them. If words for feelings referred to such locked-away objects, we couldn't talk about them at all. But we do talk — and understand one another. For Wittgenstein, the language of feelings belongs to a shared life; it grew out of how people respond to each other's pain and joy. So your feeling is not locked in an inaccessible box: it already has a shared language, and it can be shared.
loneliness.practice: Write one sentence about your feeling the way you would explain it to someone close. If you like, send it — the feeling already has a shared language.

anger.text: Duck or rabbit? The same drawing can be seen now one way, now the other, and nothing in the lines changes — Wittgenstein called this “seeing an aspect.” Anger is a strong feeling, and it often signals a crossed boundary. Anger can be such a drawing too. Extending Wittgenstein's thought, anger often holds on to one picture of a situation and won't let you see another. This doesn't mean your anger is wrong. But it's useful to notice that there are other aspects too — and sometimes that noticing alone loosens the grip a little. Wittgenstein urged, “don't think, but look!” — and that can be applied here.
anger.practice: Recall the duck-rabbit drawing and switch the aspect in your mind three times. Then try to “switch” the situation that angers you in the same way — without giving up your first view.

shame.text: Few philosophers would have dared to do what Wittgenstein did in 1937. Shame makes us hide, and it is one of the heaviest feelings — he knew it well. He was hard on himself, and one day he decided to do something he greatly feared: he wrote a “confession” and read it to close friends, admitting to acts he was ashamed of, including untruths about himself. For him this was a way to stop living with a secret. Wittgenstein would probably say: shame that stays unspoken gathers strength. Spoken, it becomes part of the shared human world. This doesn't mean you need to tell everyone. But even one honest admission — to yourself or someone close — can set you free.
shame.practice: Write on paper, in one sentence, what you are ashamed of. No one needs to see it — just let the words exist.

guilt.text: Not saying but showing — Wittgenstein believed this is how ethics works. Guilt shows that it matters to you how you've treated others — and he knew this feeling from the inside. As a young man he spent several years as a village schoolteacher in Austria and was at times harsh and rough with his pupils. Years later he went back to that village to ask some of them for forgiveness in person. This act shows how he understood guilt: not as endless self-flagellation but as a reason to do something concrete. For Wittgenstein, ethics can't be described in words; it shows itself in life — in how a person acts. This means guilt can turn from a tormenting feeling into action: admission, apology, change.
guilt.practice: If it is appropriate and safe, say one simple sentence to the person you wronged: “I was wrong.” Wittgenstein didn't theorize about guilt — he went and said it in person.

envy.text: What do chess, football and hide-and-seek have in common? Wittgenstein answered: no single thing — only a “family resemblance,” like relatives who share a nose here, a walk there. Envy arises when we forget this and measure ourselves by someone else's yardstick. In other words, “a good life” or “success” also has no single essence, no single ruler along which everyone can be lined up. When it seems that someone else “has what I don't,” we seem to assume there is only one measure. Wittgenstein would show that this is just a picture that holds us captive. Your life can be good in a completely different way.
envy.practice: Write: “For me, a good life looks like…” — and list three features that matter to you, not to anyone else.

emptiness.text: People to whom, after long doubting, the meaning of life has become clear often cannot say what it consists in — Wittgenstein wrote this striking observation into the Tractatus. If everything feels empty now and nothing moves you, that is very heavy. For him, meaning doesn't lie in the world as one more fact that can be found and put into words. It shows itself in how we live. Then emptiness does not prove there is no meaning. Perhaps it simply can't be found as the answer to a question. It may appear gradually — in small actions, in attention to things, in how you live this day.
emptiness.practice: Do one small thing slowly and attentively: brew tea, water a plant. Don't look for meaning in it — let it show itself, if it will.

confusion.text: “I don't know my way about” — this, for Wittgenstein, is the form every philosophical problem takes. Confusion, when you don't know how to go on and everything seems tangled, works the same way. He believed that muddle often arises not from a lack of information but from not seeing the whole. His answer is the “perspicuous representation”: arranging familiar things so as to see the connections between them. Nothing new needs to be added; what's already there needs to be put in a new order. If so, confusion is not a sign of stupidity but the beginning of clarification. The most important things, Wittgenstein wrote, are hidden from us by their simplicity and familiarity.
confusion.practice: List everything that is confusing you right now, one item per line. Then group the lines by theme without deciding anything — a small “perspicuous representation.”

fatigue.text: “My spade is turned” — this is how Wittgenstein described the moment when justifications run out and you hit bedrock. If you're burned out and your strength is running out, this image may unexpectedly help. And then, he wrote, I am inclined to say: “This is simply what I do.” In this light, not everything needs endless justification. Sometimes tiredness comes from constantly explaining and proving — to yourself and others — your right to something. Wittgenstein shows that the chain of justifications has an end, and that is no defeat. You can tell yourself, “Right now I need rest,” and add no proof to it.
fatigue.practice: Tell yourself: “I need rest. This is simply what I do” — and stop there, adding no “because” and no “but.” This is your bedrock.

boredom.text: “Don't think, but look!” Wittgenstein urged, convinced that what matters most is hidden from us by its simplicity and everydayness. Boredom is when everything seems familiar and uninteresting, and this call is addressed straight to it. We fail to notice something because it is always before our eyes. So boredom is not an absence of anything interesting but a habit of looking without seeing. Wittgenstein also described the “dawning of an aspect” — the moment when a familiar thing is suddenly seen anew. Such moments can't be summoned by effort, but you can open the door to them by looking at the familiar attentively, unhurriedly, without expecting that it's now supposed to become interesting.
boredom.practice: Choose an object you see every day and look at it for a minute as if for the first time. Find one detail you had never noticed.

joy.text: “The world of the happy man is a different one from that of the unhappy man,” Wittgenstein wrote in the Tractatus. A rather sombre and severe man, he knew this state too. Your joy needs no justification. In his notebooks from the First World War, which he spent at the front, there is a thought he kept returning to: the happy life is good in itself. For Wittgenstein, ethics and aesthetics are one: the good and the beautiful cannot be reduced to facts; they can only be seen. This means joy is not something that has to be explained or earned. It is a moment when the whole world opens up differently. You can simply live it, without trying to analyze it or hold on to it.
joy.practice: Step to the window or outside for a minute and look at the world through the eyes of the happy, without naming the reasons for your joy. Notice what it looks like right now.

love.text: Nobody says, “That wasn't real pain, since it passed so quickly” — but people say this about love. Wittgenstein saw an important difference here. The tenderness you feel is among the deepest experiences. Wittgenstein made an unexpected remark about love: love is not a feeling in the sense that pain is a feeling. Love is put to the test; pain is not. For Wittgenstein, love is not a fleeting sensation but something woven into life: into actions, into care, into how you treat a person over time. In other words, the tenderness you feel right now is part of a larger pattern, and its genuineness doesn't depend on how vividly you feel it at this particular minute.
love.practice: Do one small thing today for someone you love — not to tell them about the feeling but to show it.

gratitude.text: War, loneliness, severity toward himself, doubts about his work — and yet before he died, according to Norman Malcolm, Wittgenstein asked that his friends be told: “Tell them I've had a wonderful life.” Those words surprised many who knew how hard things had sometimes been for him. These are the words of someone who could see life whole, and the gratitude you feel now grows from the same ability. For Wittgenstein, gratitude doesn't require life to be easy. It is a way of seeing life whole — “sub specie aeterni,” as he put it in the Tractatus — and noticing what was good in it. Such a view doesn't cancel the difficulties, but it keeps them from blocking out everything else.
gratitude.practice: Say Wittgenstein's last words aloud: “Tell them I've had a wonderful life.” Consider what in today, however hard, might let you say the same.

quote.text: Tell them I've had a wonderful life.
quote.author: Ludwig Wittgenstein
quote.source: Last words, 1951 (as recalled by Norman Malcolm)

hope.text: “Can a dog hope?” Wittgenstein asks in the Philosophical Investigations, and the question only seems like a joke. Hope helps you keep going when the present is hard, and his answer says a lot about it. We can imagine a dog believing its master is at the door. But can it believe its master will come the day after tomorrow? Only those who have mastered language, for Wittgenstein, can hope — it takes the whole complex form of human life. Hope, for Wittgenstein, is not just a sensation inside but part of how we live with others: how we speak, make plans, wait. Then hope is not a fragile feeling that must be guarded alone. It is rooted in language and in relationships, and it can be sustained together with other people.
hope.practice: Tell someone aloud what you hope for. For Wittgenstein, hope lives in language and in relationships — put into words, it grows sturdier.

nostalgia.text: “The meaning of a word is its use in the language,” Wittgenstein taught, and language is woven into a “form of life”: habits, activities, relationships. This thought explains nostalgia, a warm sadness for the past, surprisingly well. If so, words like “home,” “summer,” “our street” were learned within a particular form of life. When it changes, the words remain, but they sound different now. Nostalgia is perhaps a longing for the form of life in which these words sounded in full. This view helps explain why nostalgia is so strong: you miss not just events but a whole world in which you lived and spoke.
nostalgia.practice: Take one word that stirs your nostalgia — “summer house,” “the yard,” “the holidays” — and ask how it was used then and how it is used now. Say both meanings aloud.

craving.text: A picture can hold us captive, Wittgenstein warned. A sharp “I want it right now” can be very strong — like a wave that rolls in and takes hold. And there is nothing shameful in it, and the wave can be waited out. In the Philosophical Investigations Wittgenstein noticed a strange thing: it seems as if a wish already knows what will satisfy it. It seems to carry within it a picture of the answer. In this light, a craving paints a very convincing picture — “this is what will help me.” But the picture is not the same as reality. You can notice this picture, acknowledge its power — and not hurry to obey. The wave of craving rises, but like any wave, it then subsides.
craving.practice: Name aloud the picture the craving paints: what exactly does it promise? Wait five minutes, breathing slowly, and notice how its strength has changed.

addiction.text: “A picture held us captive,” Wittgenstein wrote of a thought one cannot get out of because it lies in the very language we think in. Addiction is not a moral failure but a similar circle, one that becomes very strong over time. Wittgenstein also compared philosophical confusion to a fly in a fly-bottle that beats against the walls again and again, not seeing that the way out is right there. So addiction is also a stable form of life with its own habits, words and rituals. The way out is rarely found by willpower alone. More often it comes through a fresh view from outside, and through people who see the trap from the outside and can show the way.
addiction.practice: Talk about it with someone who sees the trap from outside: a friend, a professional or a mutual-help group. Wittgenstein would say: the fly is often shown the way out from outside.

hangover.text: Doubt makes sense only against the background of what we are certain of — Wittgenstein arrived at this thought in his late work On Certainty. The morning after means feeling physically unwell, and anxiety, and shame, and gaps in memory, and this thought comes in handy here. All of this is understandable, and right now you can be gentler with yourself. This means there's no point filling the gaps in memory with the worst guesses — that is not knowledge but imagination. Better to lean on what you know for sure and treat the rest as an open question. Wittgenstein also valued honest silence where nothing definite can be said. There's no need to pass sentence on yourself while there are no facts.
hangover.practice: Drink some water and write down three things you know for sure. Mark the rest simply: “don't know yet.”

euphoria.text: Everything possible and everything actual — in the Tractatus Wittgenstein distinguished “logical space” from the world of facts. Euphoria is a bright high in which everything seems open at once. Wittgenstein can help you see how this high is built. In euphoria it's as if the whole of logical space opens at once: possibilities shine, and they are real as possibilities. In other words, you can enjoy this expanse without spoiling it with doubts. Wittgenstein, however, would remind you that a possibility is not the same as a fact. This isn't a reproach but a gentle clarification: let the high be, let it fill you, but big decisions are better made once you're standing on the ground of facts again.
euphoria.practice: Write down the ideas and possibilities that seem bright right now. Set them aside for a few days before acting — let logical space meet the world of facts.

crash.text: Yesterday the drawing was a duck, today a rabbit, yet the lines are the same: Wittgenstein called this a change of aspect. A sharp drop after a high can be very unpleasant: what shone now seems gray. Nothing in the drawing itself changes — only the way we see it. And the drop is not your fault. Then after a high, the world can “switch” to another aspect, though the facts remain the same. This doesn't mean that now you see the truth and before you were deceived. Both aspects are ways of seeing the same drawing. This understanding helps you avoid hasty conclusions about your life as a whole while you're looking at it from the low point.
crash.practice: Tell yourself: “Right now I see this as…, but it's one of the aspects.” Put off serious conclusions about your life for a couple of days.

panic.text: Some words describe facts, others, like a cry, express a feeling — Wittgenstein showed how easily they get confused. A panic attack is a very frightening experience: your heart pounds, you can't get enough air, it seems something terrible is about to happen. It is neither your fault nor a flaw of character. Wittgenstein would help you see that the thought “I'm about to die” or “I'm going mad” is above all an expression of terror, its voice. This doesn't mean the terror isn't real — it is very real. But such waves usually peak and subside within a few minutes. It helps to return to simple language that everyone shares: naming objects, feeling the ground under your feet.
panic.practice: Return to simple shared language: put your feet on the floor, take a long out-breath and name five objects around you aloud with their color — “table, brown.”

dread.text: Wittgenstein, who went through the trenches of the First World War, took the question “what's it all for?” seriously. When it rises up and there seems to be an abyss beneath your feet, it is very heavy. In the Tractatus he wrote that even if science answered all its questions, the problems of life would remain completely untouched. The meaning of life, in his view, doesn't lie within the world as a fact but shows itself in how we live. He also wrote that eternal life belongs to those who live in the present. If so, the question “what for?” doesn't necessarily demand a verbal answer. Meaning may show itself in the very living of this day, in being present here and now.
dread.practice: Slowly read aloud a line from the Tractatus: “Eternal life belongs to those who live in the present.” Then for a minute simply be here: sounds, light, breath.

fomo.text: Wittgenstein taught that the meaning of words depends on the “language-game” in which they are used — and a social media feed is such a game too. The feeling that life is happening somewhere else is born largely from its rules. In this game someone always looks happier. But these are the rules of a game, not a description of reality. Wittgenstein would show that you can step out of the game by seeing it as a game. Your own life isn't losing the competition, because it doesn't have to take part in it at all. Its meaning is made of your own language-games — conversations, work, attachments that never make it into the feed.
fomo.practice: Imagine describing your day not for the feed but to a close friend — and say those three sentences to yourself. In which game does your life look different?

sleepless.text: The engine turns over but drives nothing — this is how Wittgenstein described language that is “idling.” At night, when you can't sleep and thoughts go round and round, everything seems scarier. In this light, nighttime thoughts are often exactly this kind of idling. They look like reflections on important matters, but they resolve nothing and can't resolve anything at three in the morning. This doesn't mean your worries are unimportant — just that night is not the place for them. Wittgenstein would show that noticing the mind is idling is already a way of loosening it a little. In the morning the same worries can be looked at, when language is “working” again, that is, connected to things that can be done.
sleepless.practice: If thoughts keep circling, tell yourself: “This is idling.” Write one thought on a slip of paper and set it aside until morning.

betrayal.text: “If I want the door to turn, the hinges must stay put,” Wittgenstein wrote in On Certainty. Trust in those close to us is one of these hinges, which is why betrayal wounds so deeply. This pain is not only about a person but about the ground you stood on. It's impossible not to trust at all: must I not begin to trust somewhere? So betrayal hurts so much because one of the hinges your life turned on has been torn off. This doesn't mean you were naive. Trust is not a mistake but a necessary condition of life. It will take time to find new supports, and there's no need to rush yourself into deciding whom to trust again, and when.
betrayal.practice: Write down whom and what in your life you can still trust. Even if the list is short, these are your hinges.

jealousy.text: “An inner process stands in need of outward criteria,” Wittgenstein wrote, arguing against the picture of the soul as a locked box. Jealousy is an agonizing mix of love, fear and imagined pictures, and this thought bears on it directly. This means jealousy often rests on exactly that picture — as if somewhere inside the other person a secret truth were hidden that we must uncover. But for Wittgenstein, the inner shows itself in the outer: in words, actions, the way someone treats you. You can rely on what is seen and said, rather than on the imagined contents of someone else's “box.” This doesn't cancel jealousy or make it shameful — it shows how dear the person is to you. But relying on what is visible makes it a little less all-powerful.
jealousy.practice: Note on paper what you actually saw and heard, separately from what you assume. Look at both parts.

resentment.text: Language seems to repeat the same picture to us relentlessly — this is how Wittgenstein described a captivity that is hard to escape. Long-held resentment is hard to carry: it's as if it had moved in and settled inside. Wittgenstein believed philosophy helps us see such a picture from outside — and then its power weakens. In other words, resentment is often stored as a sentence we repeat to ourselves again and again. Each repetition makes it sturdier. This doesn't mean the resentment is unjustified — you really were hurt. But you can notice that you carry around not only the event but also certain words about it. Sometimes changing the words helps loosen the grip a little.
resentment.practice: Jot down the sentence you usually use to retell the hurt to yourself. Try to rephrase it more neutrally, without cancelling the pain.

heartbreak.text: Words live within a “form of life” — habits, activities, relationships — Wittgenstein taught. When a relationship ends, it is one of the sharpest pains, and Wittgenstein helps explain why it hurts so much. Then in the relationship you had a shared language — the words “we” and “ours,” special jokes and names. After a breakup these words lose their game: there's no one to share them with. This is one of the reasons a breakup hurts so much — part of your language leaves along with the person. This understanding doesn't lessen the pain, but it explains it: you're losing not only a person but a whole world of meanings. In time a new language will appear, but grieving the old one is natural.
heartbreak.practice: Write down one word or phrase that belonged only to the two of you. Allow yourself to grieve for it.

impostor.text: “Now I know how to go on!” — for Wittgenstein, understanding consists precisely in this ability to go on, not in an inner sensation. The feeling that you don't actually understand anything and are about to be found out doesn't hold up well against this thought. Wittgenstein wrote that we shouldn't think of understanding as a “mental process.” Understanding shows itself in knowing how to go on — in what you do, apply, solve. If so, you don't need to feel like a “real expert” in order to be one. Your competence is visible in your work, not in whether you have confidence inside. The absence of that feeling says nothing about your skill.
impostor.practice: Recall three things you actually did recently and name them aloud — not how you feel, but what you did. That is your “I know how to go on.”

self_hatred.text: Wittgenstein, who was himself very hard on himself, taught us to ask of any sentence: how does it work? The inner critic can be cruel, and its voice is hard to hear. Wittgenstein himself heard a merciless inner voice for years. Some describe facts; others are moves in a game: judgments, verdicts, orders. In this light, the sentence “I'm worthless” looks like the description of a fact, but in reality it is a move in a particular game — the game of self-condemnation. It is not the truth about you but a verdict handed down according to rules you can examine from the outside. Once you notice this, you can step back a little from the critic's voice. It speaks loudly, but that doesn't make its words true.
self_hatred.practice: Take one sentence of your inner critic and ask, as Wittgenstein would: how is this word used? Who says this, when, and in what game? Is it a description — or a verdict?

helplessness.text: “The world is independent of my will,” Wittgenstein wrote in the Tractatus, and it sounds grim until you read the thought to the end. Helplessness is a heavy feeling, when it seems you can't change anything. But Wittgenstein carries the thought further: the will doesn't change the facts of the world, but it can change its limits — how the world is seen as a whole. So even if outward circumstances are beyond your power, your attitude toward them, the way you meet them, remains yours. This doesn't mean you should simply resign yourself. But the experience of helplessness doesn't cancel the fact that you still have inner freedom — in how you see, and in small actions.
helplessness.practice: Take three slow breaths in and out and notice: your breath, your gaze, what you are looking at — these are still yours. For Wittgenstein, the will changes not the facts but how the world is seen.

procrastination.text: “In the beginning was the deed” — Wittgenstein quotes this line from Goethe in On Certainty, and it sounds like advice to someone who can't get started. It seems you first need to understand and plan everything. Wittgenstein also showed that understanding a rule shows itself not in holding it in your head but in beginning to act and being able to go on. This means you don't need to fully understand how to do the task before you begin. Understanding comes along the way. The first step, even an unsure one, is already part of understanding. Wittgenstein described the moment when a person suddenly says, “Now I know how to go on!” — and that moment often comes only after you've begun.
procrastination.practice: Take the smallest first step — open the file, type one sentence — and see whether that “now I know how to go on” arrives.

uprooted.text: Vienna, Manchester, Cambridge, Norway, Ireland — Wittgenstein moved a great deal and wrote in German while living surrounded by English. Being cut off from home, especially when you have to live in a foreign language, was familiar to him. A move is not only a change of address, and he understood well why. For him, language is not just a set of words but part of a “form of life.” In other words, when you move, you lose not only a place but a whole world of meanings, of language-games in which you belonged. This explains why emigration is so hard. But Wittgenstein also shows something else: new forms of life can be mastered, new games can be learned — gradually, step by step — and your world will grow wider.
uprooted.practice: Today, ask someone local how one local word or expression is used — and try saying it yourself. This, for Wittgenstein, is how a new language-game is learned.

quote.text: The limits of my language mean the limits of my world.
quote.author: Ludwig Wittgenstein

overload.text: A small hut above a Norwegian fjord, where news barely reached — this is where Wittgenstein went to think. When there is too much information and too many demands, the mind gets overloaded, and this picture may help. Wittgenstein valued clarity. In the preface to the Tractatus he wrote that what can be said at all can be said clearly. Then overload is a sign that there's too much that is unclear and superfluous in your head. Wittgenstein would show that not everything needs to be let in, and that what matters can be seen once the superfluous is set aside. Sometimes clarity comes not from new information but from silence and simplicity — from ceasing to let in the new and looking at what is already there.
overload.practice: Switch off all screens for five minutes and sit in silence, as if in Wittgenstein's Norwegian hut. Let your thoughts simply settle.

unreality.text: “If you tried to doubt everything you would not get as far as doubting anything,” Wittgenstein wrote in On Certainty. The feeling that everything is somehow not real can be very strange and unsettling, and this sentence speaks directly to it. There are things we lean on without even noticing. If so, even when the world seems unreal, your body, your language and your familiar actions go on leaning on the world. This feeling doesn't make you strange. You can gently return to simple supports — objects, sounds, words — not arguing with the feeling, just touching again and again what you lean on.
unreality.practice: Touch something with a noticeable texture and say aloud what it is and how it feels. Repeat with two or three objects — these are your supports.

awe.text: “How extraordinary that the world should exist” — in his “Lecture on Ethics” (1929) Wittgenstein called this experience his chief example of absolute value. Awe before something vast or beautiful is a rare and valuable feeling, and he knew it. For this experience, he thought, there are no fitting words — and none are needed. For him this feeling went beyond what can be put into words and belonged to what he called “the mystical.” This is not superstition but an acknowledgment that there are things that show themselves but can't be described. In this light, awe doesn't need explaining. You can simply live it, letting yourself wonder that all this exists.
awe.practice: Keep your eyes on what stirred your awe for one more minute. Tell yourself: “How extraordinary that this exists.”

quote.text: Not how the world is, is the mystical, but that it is.
quote.author: Ludwig Wittgenstein

relief.text: “What is your aim in philosophy? To show the fly the way out of the fly-bottle,” Wittgenstein wrote. Relief is a warm wave when the heaviness lifts. Imagine what the fly feels at the moment it finally flies out into freedom. So relief is the moment when what seemed unsolvable suddenly comes untied. Interestingly, for Wittgenstein the way out often turns out to be simple and was nearby all along — it just couldn't be seen from inside the trap. Relief is not just the absence of heaviness but a small liberation, and there's nothing in it that has to be analyzed or earned right away. Don't rush on to the next worry: this moment is worth noticing and living fully.
relief.practice: Take a deep breath in and a slow breath out. Tell yourself: “It's easier now” — and stay with it one more minute, like the fly that has flown free.

calm.text: The real discovery, Wittgenstein wrote, is the one that gives philosophy peace, so that it is no longer tormented by questions that bring itself into question. Calm is a precious state, and right now you have it. Wittgenstein also said that philosophy “leaves everything as it is” — it doesn't change the world but helps us see it clearly. This means calm is not the absence of thoughts but a moment when thoughts no longer pull in different directions. In the Tractatus he linked true life with living in the present. You can simply be in this calm without trying to analyze it or asking how long it will last. Wittgenstein would probably say that calm needs no explanation: it shows itself.
calm.practice: Stay in this state a little longer. Notice how your body feels without trying to change anything: “leave everything as it is.”

inspiration.text: Wittgenstein built his books out of short remarks that he rearranged for years, like index cards. He knew well the moment when thoughts come freely and you want to act. Wittgenstein described how a person suddenly exclaims, “Now I know how to go on!” — when before, something wasn't working. He also described the “dawning of an aspect”: a familiar thing is suddenly seen anew. In other words, inspiration is a moment when you see a new aspect, a new connection. You can catch it by writing it down at once and put it in order later. Wittgenstein didn't wait for final clarity before writing: his Philosophical Investigations is a collection of such caught moments, which he rearranged and polished for years. You can start with a rough note.
inspiration.practice: Write down the thought that has come as a numbered remark — “1.”, as Wittgenstein did — without editing. It can be put in order later.

schadenfreude.text: German, Wittgenstein's native language, found a separate word for this feeling — Schadenfreude, literally “joy in harm.” It's awkward to admit even to yourself, and yet it is very human. Wittgenstein taught that the meaning of a word lies in its use, in how it is woven into our shared life, which he called a “form of life.” Then since language has found a name for this feeling, people must have known it for a long time — it's not your personal monstrousness but a recognizable pattern of human life. Wittgenstein also stressed that feelings show themselves in what a person does. A fleeting spark of schadenfreude says nothing about you yet. What matters more is what you do next.
schadenfreude.practice: Name the feeling to yourself calmly, like the weather: “this is schadenfreude.” Then ask: which hurt of my own has echoed here?

contempt.text: Sharp in his judgments, Wittgenstein could demolish someone in a single sentence, and in his diaries he repeatedly reproached himself for vanity and arrogance. Contempt can be cold and even pleasant: it places us above others. His philosophy offers an unexpected key. He wrote about “pictures” that hold us captive: one image starts to seem like the whole truth. Contempt is exactly such a picture: “he's simply a nobody.” Wittgenstein also taught us to notice “aspects”: in one drawing you can see now a duck, now a rabbit. If so, contempt is a frozen gaze in which a person is seen from one side only. You don't need to force yourself to respect them. It's enough to notice that this is an aspect, not the whole person — and to ask what this contempt is protecting in you.
contempt.practice: Think of the person you feel contempt for and find one trait in them that can be seen differently — not better, just differently, like the duck and the rabbit in one drawing.

disgust.text: One word, different games: Wittgenstein would note that we use “disgust” in very different ways. It is a strong bodily feeling — you want to turn away, to move back — and it can concern people, a situation, even yourself. Disgust at a smell, at hypocrisy and at yourself are different “language-games,” that is, different ways of using the word in life, linked only by “family resemblance.” Mixing them up, it's easy to get confused. Disgust at a situation can be an honest signal: something here is unacceptable to you. But self-disgust often merely borrows the language of bodily revulsion to pass a verdict. Wittgenstein would suggest not arguing with the feeling but clarifying which game it is sounding in right now. Clarity alone lifts part of the weight.
disgust.practice: Complete the sentence in writing: “I'm disgusted because…” — and see what it is really about: the body, your values, or a verdict on yourself.

revenge.text: A person kisses a picture of someone they love not because they believe the picture will feel anything — in his “Remarks on Frazer's Golden Bough,” Wittgenstein saw such gestures as the expression of a feeling, and found their satisfaction in that. The desire for revenge is a natural response to pain inflicted on you: you were treated unjustly, and that is important to acknowledge. There is no need to be ashamed of this feeling, and Wittgenstein can help you see what it is really looking for. In this light, the desire for revenge is often, above all, a need to express that what happened was wrong. This need can be respected and satisfied through expression without harming anyone — through words, a letter you won't send, acknowledging the pain before someone who will understand.
revenge.practice: Write a letter to the person who hurt you that you will not send. Say everything in it — then keep it or tear it up.

anger_at_loved.text: Quick-tempered and harsh with his closest friends, Wittgenstein knew how to come back afterwards and admit he was wrong. Snapping at someone you love and then being tormented by it is one of the most common and most shameful experiences. Wittgenstein objected to the habit of thinking that behind a word there is one hidden essence that can be checked at any single moment. He noted that love is not a sensation like pain: it is tested by life. So love shows itself in the whole pattern of life with a person, over time, and a flash of anger is an episode in that pattern, not a refutation of love. Anger often shows where you feel cramped or hurt. It doesn't need to be turned against the person you love — it can be understood and named.
anger_at_loved.practice: When the anger subsides, finish the sentence aloud: “I got angry because I needed…” — and, if you can, calmly say it to your loved one.

ambivalence.text: A duck and a rabbit in one drawing — and neither way of seeing is the only correct one, Wittgenstein taught. To love and to be unable to stand the same person is agonizing, and you want to understand what you “really” feel. It is a very common state. Wittgenstein showed that such a question can be a trap. He called this “seeing aspects.” This means a person close to you can evoke both tenderness and irritation, and both feelings are true — they are different aspects of the same relationship. The demand that only one remain is a “picture” that holds you captive. Allowing yourself both feelings, you stop being at war with yourself.
ambivalence.practice: Say two sentences to yourself: “What I love in you is…” and “It's hard for me with you when…”. Don't choose between them — like the duck and the rabbit, let both be visible.

guilty_relief.text: A “one-sided diet” — examples of only one kind — was for Wittgenstein the main cause of philosophical illness. Relief after a hard ending — a breakup, the end of a loved one's long illness — often comes with shame: “how can I feel relief?” Wittgenstein noticed that words for feelings don't work like labels on separate objects: “grief,” he wrote, describes a pattern that recurs, with different variations, in the weave of life. In other words, grief, love, tiredness and relief can be interwoven in a single pattern. Relief means that a long strain has ended, not that you didn't love. Your experience is wider than the single sentence “if I feel relieved, I must be a bad person.”
guilty_relief.practice: Tell yourself: “I feel lighter — and I loved.” Stay with the fact that both statements can be true at once.

indifference.text: Grammar, for Wittgenstein, is not school rules but how a word actually lives in our lives. Sometimes you're not moved by what “should” move you, and anxiety is added to the indifference: is something wrong with me? Wittgenstein criticized the idea that every word for a feeling must have an inner “flash” that can be checked by looking inside yourself. He wrote that an “inner process” stands in need of outward criteria. Then the absence of a vivid sensation at this minute doesn't yet mean you don't care. Care can live in actions, in memory, in attention. And sometimes indifference is simply tiredness, or protection when there have been too many feelings. The “should” here is someone else's grammar. You don't have to feel on schedule.
indifference.practice: Recall one small action by which you recently took care of someone or something. Notice: care can be quiet.

quote.text: An “inner process” stands in need of outward criteria.
quote.author: Ludwig Wittgenstein

escape.text: Wittgenstein dropped everything more than once: he gave away an enormous inheritance, became a village teacher, worked as a gardener's assistant at a monastery, lived for long stretches in a hut in Norway, left his chair at Cambridge. The wish to drop everything — a job, a city, a role — says something important. This was not a flight from life but a search for a place where he could live and think honestly. By his logic, sometimes a difficulty can't be resolved within the old “language-game,” and the game itself — the form of life — needs to change. But it's useful to ask what exactly you want to leave and what you want to come to. Sometimes a small change is enough, sometimes a big step is needed — and there's no need to hurry.
escape.practice: Imagine for a minute that you have already “changed the game.” What would you do differently on the first day of the new life? Perhaps some of it is available in the old one too.

forbidden_attraction.text: “Whereof one cannot speak, thereof one must be silent” — the last line of the Tractatus, but Wittgenstein meant not a ban but respect for what only shows itself. Attraction to someone unavailable or “wrong” is disorienting: the feeling is there, but there's no place for it, and this doesn't make you a bad person. Wittgenstein also doubted that by looking inside yourself you could simply “read” your desire, like an inscription on a sign. If so, attraction is neither a verdict nor a command. It may show something about you: a longing for aliveness, for attention, for another life. The question is not only “whom do I want?” but also “what does this desire mean to me?” Wittgenstein wouldn't pass judgment — he would suggest looking attentively, without hurrying to conclusions and without demanding immediate clarity of yourself.
forbidden_attraction.practice: Walk for a few minutes and ask yourself on the way, without judging: what does this attraction seem to ask for in my life — attention, lightness, risk, tenderness? One word is enough.

social_anxiety.text: The Cambridge dons seemed like strangers to Wittgenstein, and he seemed a difficult companion to them. Fear of people and their judgment can freeze you so that it's hard to get a word out, and he knew this. His philosophy contains a thought that may help. He wrote: “My attitude towards him is an attitude towards a soul.” We see one another not as machines handing out grades but as living people with fears of their own. The fear of judgment paints a one-sided “picture”: as if everyone around were a judge. Wittgenstein might remark: this picture holds you captive, but it isn't the only one. The people nearby are most likely a little afraid too — and also in need of a kindly gaze.
social_anxiety.practice: At your next gathering, choose one person and quietly notice something alive in them: a gesture, tiredness, a smile. You are not only being looked at — you are looking too.

uncertainty.text: What stays solid when much is shaking? Wittgenstein devoted his last work, On Certainty, to this question. Uncertainty is exhausting: it's unclear what will happen, and there's nothing to lean on. Wittgenstein noticed that doubt is possible only against the background of what we don't doubt. He compared such foundations to a riverbed: the water of changing opinions flows along it, and the bed itself can gradually shift too, but not all at once. Extending Wittgenstein's thought, even amid great uncertainty, much remains solid — your hands, your language, the people you know, the simple skills of living. The future is unclear, but you are not standing in a void. Noticing the riverbed makes it easier to withstand the current.
uncertainty.practice: List on paper the five simplest things you don't doubt right now. This is your riverbed.

quote.text: If you tried to doubt everything you would not get as far as doubting anything. The game of doubting itself presupposes certainty.
quote.author: Ludwig Wittgenstein

waiting.text: Wittgenstein seriously asked what waiting is, and noticed that it is not one inner sensation lasting the whole time. When you wait for an answer, results, news, time stretches out and can become agonizing, especially when the outcome is not up to you. When you're expecting a guest, you look at the clock, put the kettle on, listen for footsteps: expectation is woven into the situation and into actions. In this light, waiting is not only torment inside but also what you do while you wait. And that, at least in part, can be chosen. Waiting doesn't require you to hold the question in your head constantly: the answer will come even if, for a while, you turn to something else.
waiting.practice: Fill the next hour with one small task that has nothing to do with the waiting — put the kettle on, as if for a guest — and do it slowly.

quote.text: An expectation is embedded in a situation, from which it arises.
quote.author: Ludwig Wittgenstein

regret.text: Wittgenstein knew the past can't be changed — and yet one day he did the one thing that was possible with it. Regret over something done or left undone can return again and again. In the 1920s, working as a village schoolteacher, he was sometimes cruel to his pupils and struck them. Years later he returned to the village and personally asked some of his former pupils for forgiveness. It was very hard for him, but he considered it necessary. Wittgenstein would probably say: regret is not only a gnawing thought; it can show itself in an act. The past can't be changed, but you can change what you do with it today. And a big gesture isn't always needed: sometimes it's enough to honestly admit the mistake and act differently next time.
regret.practice: Choose one small action in which your regret can “show itself” today — even if it is just an honest admission to yourself.

longing.text: Could someone feel ardent love for just one second — regardless of what came before or after? Wittgenstein answered: no. Missing a particular person hurts in a special way: it's precisely their voice, their habits you miss. Wittgenstein asked such questions not as a game of wit but to understand how our feelings work. Such feelings make sense only within a whole story, surrounded by a life. So your longing is not just an unpleasant sensation you'd like to switch off. It is a sign of how deeply this person is woven into your life. Longing speaks of connection. You can carry it as part of that story, not as a mistake that needs fixing.
longing.practice: Recall one concrete detail of this person — a gesture, a phrase, a scent. Let yourself simply remember it.

world_pain.text: Wittgenstein went to the First World War as a volunteer, was on the front line and in captivity, and it was in his wartime notebooks that the Tractatus took shape. Pain for the world — from hard news, wars, injustice — was something he knew first-hand. Wittgenstein wrote that the sense of the world lies outside the world of facts, and that ethics cannot be put into words but shows itself. This means you don't have to find words that explain the world's suffering — there may be none. But your attitude toward the world shows itself in how you live: in kindness to those near you, in honesty, in whatever help you can give. That is no small thing. It is exactly what cannot be said but can be shown.
world_pain.practice: Choose one small kind act today — for someone close or for a stranger. Not as a solution to the world's problems, but as your answer to them.

rejection.text: Language can lead us astray, Wittgenstein warned, and a refusal is a good example. Rejection wounds deeply: it seems a verdict has been passed on you. The phrase “I was rejected” sounds like a statement about you, as if someone had measured your worth. But for Wittgenstein, the meaning of words lies in their use. When you weren't chosen, that was another person's action in a particular situation, within their “language-game” — with its own rules, needs and history. It is not a description of who you are. If you didn't get the job, or someone didn't return your feelings, that speaks of an encounter, not of your essence. You can let yourself grieve without turning the grief into a final verdict on yourself.
rejection.practice: Say the phrase “I was rejected” more precisely: “This person, in this situation, decided…” Notice how its weight changes.

abandonment.text: A child first believes and only later learns to doubt — this is how Wittgenstein, in On Certainty, described where our trust comes from. The fear of being abandoned strikes right here, and it can be very strong, especially if you have been left before. Trust is not a conclusion drawn from evidence but the ground on which anything becomes possible at all. In other words, the fear of abandonment is a crack in that ground. That is why trying to prove to yourself that you won't be left often doesn't help: no proof can replace trust. But trust can be grown again, step by step, in relationships with people who stay. Your fear is understandable, and it doesn't mean you will necessarily be left.
abandonment.practice: Think of someone who stayed by you though they could have left. Write down one thing they did for you.

unrequited.text: Any language-game takes at least two — Wittgenstein saw language as a shared practice. Unrequited love is a pain that is hard to share: the feeling is enormous, and there is no answer. Wittgenstein wrote that love is not a sensation like pain: it is tested by life, by actions, by time. Then your love is real, but the shared “game” in which it would have been answered didn't come together. This doesn't mean you loved wrongly or that you are unworthy of love. It means that reciprocity takes two — and that is not in your power. You can respect your feeling and at the same time allow it, in time, to find another form.
unrequited.practice: Put down on paper what this love has taught you about yourself — one thing that will stay with you.

humiliation.text: Who sets the rules of the game? This simple question of Wittgenstein's sheds much light on humiliation — an experience that leaves a deep mark: you were made to look worthless, and it seems everyone saw it. Wittgenstein showed that words and gestures take on meaning within “language-games” — shared rules by which people act. Humiliation is a game in which one person claims the right to decide who is worth what. For Wittgenstein, you didn't set the rules of this game, and you don't have to accept them as a description of reality. The fact that you were humiliated speaks of the game you were drawn into, not of your essence. Wittgenstein saw the task of philosophy as showing the fly the way out of the fly-bottle. Sometimes it's enough to see that you've been caught in the trap of someone else's rules in order to start getting out.
humiliation.practice: Jot down the “rules” by which you were humiliated. Then write the rule by which you would want people to treat one another.

body_shame.text: “The human body is the best picture of the human soul,” Wittgenstein wrote. If dissatisfaction with your body has become a constant background — the mirror, photos, other people's glances — this sentence may sound surprising. You are not alone in this feeling. Wittgenstein meant that we see joy, sadness and attention right in a face and in gestures: the body is not a shell but the place where the soul becomes visible. If so, judging the body only as appearance, by the standards of advertising, means looking at it through one narrow “picture.” Your body is how you laugh, hug, get tired, hold a cup. It is a living expression of you, not an object for an exam.
body_shame.practice: Recall one movement of your body that expresses you — a gesture, your walk, your laugh. Stay with this image for a minute: it is a picture of your soul.

quote.text: The human body is the best picture of the human soul.
quote.author: Ludwig Wittgenstein
quote.source: Philosophical Investigations, Part II, section iv

illness.text: Wittgenstein wrote his last notes for On Certainty when he was already seriously ill: he worked as much as his strength allowed. Illness changes a great deal — the body you relied on suddenly lets you down — and your fear and weariness here are legitimate. Wittgenstein reflected on what remains certain when much is shaking: on the simple things life rests on. Wittgenstein might remark: illness doesn't reset your life to zero; it changes its “game,” its rules. But even in the new game there is room for meaning, thought, connection with people. Wittgenstein made of his illness neither a tragedy nor a feat — he went on living and thinking as best he could.
illness.practice: Notice one thing you were able to do today, however small. It too is part of your life.

pride.text: Few would dare to call their famous book mistaken in public and still not disown it — Wittgenstein dared. Pride in what you've done is a healthy, good feeling: you have accomplished something, and that deserves acknowledgment. Wittgenstein had plenty to be proud of: his Tractatus immediately became an event in philosophy. But he was demanding of himself and later revised many of its ideas. In the preface to the Philosophical Investigations he openly admitted the “grave mistakes” of his first book — and yet he didn't disown it, suggesting that the two books be read side by side. Extending Wittgenstein's thought, healthy pride doesn't require the result to be final and flawless. You can be proud of what you've done and remain open to growing further. One doesn't cancel the other. Let yourself be glad: this is yours.
pride.practice: Tell someone what you've done in one or two sentences — without caveats or downplaying. You can be proud and stay open to growing.

melancholy.text: Wittgenstein could whistle whole movements of symphonies from memory and was convinced that the meaning of music couldn't be retold in words. Gentle sadness is a subtle feeling in which sorrow lives alongside tenderness and beauty. Wittgenstein distinguished what can be said from what only shows itself. In this light, melancholy is one of those feelings that are hard to explain but show themselves clearly in a melody, in autumn light, in a memory. It doesn't need to be “solved” or fixed. Wittgenstein wrote that philosophy “leaves everything as it is.” Sometimes a feeling, too, is best allowed to be just as it is — quiet, a little sad, and alive.
melancholy.practice: Put on music that answers this mood and simply listen, without trying to change anything.
